2026-12-30.title: Wednesday after the First Sunday after Yaldo
readings: He will be called a Nazorean
2026-12-30.verse: May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.
theo: After Herod's death an angel tells Joseph in a dream to return with the child and his mother to the land of Israel. Fearing Herod's son Archelaus, he settles in Galilee, in Nazareth, “so that what had been spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled, ‘He will be called a Nazorean.’” Like Israel, the child is called out of Egypt; like a hidden shoot, he grows up in an obscure village. Joseph's quiet obedience protects the life of the Saviour.

Paul tells Jews and Gentiles in Rome: “Welcome one another, therefore, just as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God.” Christ became a servant to Israel to confirm the promises, and the Gentiles glorify God for his mercy; Isaiah's “root of Jesse” rises to rule the nations, “in him the Gentiles shall hope.” At the end of the year, Paul's blessing is perfect: “May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing.”
outline: Who needs our welcome as the year ends?
“May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace.”
live: Welcome a migrant or newcomer in your parish or neighbourhood.

2026-12-30.prayer: God of hope, you brought your Son out of Egypt and hid him in Nazareth. Fill us with joy and peace in believing, teach us to welcome one another as Christ welcomed us, and make us abound in hope by the power of your Spirit. Amen.

pm.open: God of hope, fill us with all joy and peace in believing. As we gather near the end of the year, teach us to welcome one another as Christ welcomed us. Amen.

illus: A Malankara Catholic family that moved from Kerala to Bengaluru found their new parish full of strangers. On their first Sunday an elderly couple invited them home for lunch. Twenty years later, the family says: “That lunch was our Nazareth.”

homily: Dear friends, St Paul tells the Romans: welcome one another, therefore, just as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God (Romans 15:7). Christ welcomed us when we were far from him. We are called to welcome others the same way.

Paul gathers several Scriptures to show that Christ came for the Gentiles as well as for Israel, and ends with Isaiah: the root of Jesse shall come, the one who rises to rule the Gentiles; in him the Gentiles shall hope. Then he prays: may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope by the power of the Holy Spirit (Romans 15:12–13).

In the Gospel, after Herod's death, an angel tells Joseph in a dream to return to the land of Israel. But fearing Herod's son, Joseph is warned again and goes to Galilee, settling in a town called Nazareth (Matthew 2:19–23).

The Holy Family's life was not settled. Exile in Egypt, return, fear, another change of plan. Joseph had to listen to God again and again. Yet in all this, the family stayed together and the Child grew.
Many of our families live like this: moving for work, uncertain futures, plans that change. The God of hope walks with us. He led Joseph step by step, and he leads us.
As the year ends, let us welcome one another as Christ welcomed us, especially those far from home. And let us ask the God of hope to fill us with joy and peace for the year to come. Amen.
